clinicalPearls: A rare, highly aggressive renal malignancy that arises from the collecting duct epithelium of the renal medulla
Occurs almost exclusively in young people with sickle cell trait, and less often with sickle cell disease or other haemoglobinopathies
Typically presents with haematuria, flank or abdominal pain, and a palpable mass, often with weight loss
Most patients have metastatic disease at diagnosis, commonly to lymph nodes, lung, liver and bone
Tumours characteristically show loss of the SMARCB1 (INI1) tumour-suppressor protein on immunohistochemistry
It should be suspected in any young Black patient with sickle cell trait who presents with a renal mass
Prognosis is poor and it responds poorly to conventional targeted agents used in clear cell disease
reference.pathophysiology: Renal medullary carcinoma arises from the distal collecting duct or calyceal epithelium within the renal medulla. The chronic hypoxic, hypertonic medullary environment in individuals with sickling haemoglobinopathies is thought to promote genomic instability and malignant transformation. Loss of function of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling subunit SMARCB1 (INI1) is a defining molecular event, driving an aggressive, poorly differentiated tumour with early lymphovascular invasion and rapid metastatic spread.
additionalDifferentials: Urothelial carcinoma of the upper tract
High-grade clear cell renal cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis to characterise the mass and assess spread
Cross-sectional imaging of chest for pulmonary metastases
Tissue biopsy with immunohistochemistry, including SMARCB1 (INI1) staining
Haemoglobinopathy testing (sickle solubility test and haemoglobin electrophoresis)
Baseline bloods including renal function and markers of tumour burden
redFlags: Visible haematuria with a renal mass in a young patient with sickle cell trait
Rapidly enlarging mass with systemic symptoms
Evidence of widespread metastatic disease at presentation
Bone pain or pathological fracture suggesting skeletal spread
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with most patients presenting with advanced disease and short survival; localised disease treated with surgery combined with systemic chemotherapy offers the best, though still limited, outcomes.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis in a young patient because renal cancer is assumed to affect older adults
Failing to test for sickle cell trait when a medullary renal mass is found
Misclassifying it as clear cell carcinoma and offering ineffective targeted therapy
Delaying tissue diagnosis in a rapidly progressive tumour
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Platinum-based cytotoxic chemotherapy is the systemic mainstay for this aggressive SMARCB1-deficient tumour, which is largely resistant to conventional targeted agents
Radical nephrectomy for localised disease, ideally combined with systemic chemotherapy given the high rate of early micrometastatic spread
Deliver care with prompt, upfront multimodal treatment because most patients present with metastatic disease and survival is short
Provide palliative and supportive care, including symptom control, radiotherapy for painful metastases and management of tumour burden, for advanced disease
Confirm the underlying sickle cell trait or haemoglobinopathy and give supportive haematological care to reduce medullary sickling stress
Refer for genetic counselling and family sickle screening, since the tumour arises almost exclusively in those with sickling haemoglobinopathies
Manage through a uro-oncology multidisciplinary team and consider clinical trial enrolment given the poor response to standard therapy
